claim: Beta band oscillations are typically defined as 13–30 Hz.
source: Beta band oscillations (typically defined as 13–30 Hz) have been noted to reliably emerge during specific motor actions such as isometric contraction and precision reaching, after movement-related cues, and prior to instructed reaches (Baker et al., 2003, Baker et al., 1997; Canolty et al., 2012; Engel and Fries, 2010; Leventhal et al., 2012; Saleh et al., 2010; Sanes and Donoghue, 1993).
evidence: The manuscript provides a direct definition of beta band oscillations with citation support.

claim: Beta band oscillations reliably emerge during isometric contraction and precision reaching.
source: Beta band oscillations (typically defined as 13–30 Hz) have been noted to reliably emerge during specific motor actions such as isometric contraction and precision reaching, after movement-related cues, and prior to instructed reaches (Baker et al., 2003, Baker et al., 1997; Canolty et al., 2012; Engel and Fries, 2010; Leventhal et al., 2012; Saleh et al., 2010; Sanes and Donoghue, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Beta oscillations have been hypothesized to indicate ongoing sensorimotor integration.
source: The most prominent of these hypotheses suggest beta oscillations indicate ongoing sensorimotor integration (Baker, 2007), coordination (Rubino et al., 2006), idling (Engel and Fries, 2010; Gilbertson et al., 2005; Pfurtscheller et al., 1996), motor preparation (Donoghue et al., 1998), or attention (Fetz, 2013; Saleh et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to Baker, 2007.

claim: Beta oscillations have been hypothesized to indicate coordination.
source: The most prominent of these hypotheses suggest beta oscillations indicate ongoing sensorimotor integration (Baker, 2007), coordination (Rubino et al., 2006), idling (Engel and Fries, 2010; Gilbertson et al., 2005; Pfurtscheller et al., 1996), motor preparation (Donoghue et al., 1998), or attention (Fetz, 2013; Saleh et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to Rubino et al., 2006.

claim: Beta oscillations have been hypothesized to indicate idling.
source: The most prominent of these hypotheses suggest beta oscillations indicate ongoing sensorimotor integration (Baker, 2007), coordination (Rubino et al., 2006), idling (Engel and Fries, 2010; Gilbertson et al., 2005; Pfurtscheller et al., 1996), motor preparation (Donoghue et al., 1998), or attention (Fetz, 2013; Saleh et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Engel and Fries, 2010; Gilbertson et al., 2005; Pfurtscheller et al., 1996.

claim: Beta oscillations have been hypothesized to indicate motor preparation.
source: The most prominent of these hypotheses suggest beta oscillations indicate ongoing sensorimotor integration (Baker, 2007), coordination (Rubino et al., 2006), idling (Engel and Fries, 2010; Gilbertson et al., 2005; Pfurtscheller et al., 1996), motor preparation (Donoghue et al., 1998), or attention (Fetz, 2013; Saleh et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to Donoghue et al., 1998.

claim: Beta oscillations have been hypothesized to indicate attention.
source: The most prominent of these hypotheses suggest beta oscillations indicate ongoing sensorimotor integration (Baker, 2007), coordination (Rubino et al., 2006), idling (Engel and Fries, 2010; Gilbertson et al., 2005; Pfurtscheller et al., 1996), motor preparation (Donoghue et al., 1998), or attention (Fetz, 2013; Saleh et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Fetz, 2013; Saleh et al., 2010.

claim: Slowly oscillating cortical macrostimulation (up to 1.7 Hz) has been shown to entrain single unit neural activity in anesthetized rodents.
source: Slowly oscillating cortical macrostimulation (up to 1.7 Hz) has been shown to entrain single unit neural activity in anesthetized rodents, although this entrainment was overpowered by endogenous rhythms in an awake situation (Ozen et al., 2010; Venkatraman and Carmena, 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Entrainment from slowly oscillating cortical macrostimulation was overpowered by endogenous rhythms in awake rodents.
source: Slowly oscillating cortical macrostimulation (up to 1.7 Hz) has been shown to entrain single unit neural activity in anesthetized rodents, although this entrainment was overpowered by endogenous rhythms in an awake situation (Ozen et al., 2010; Venkatraman and Carmena, 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Non-invasive stimulation via tACS and rTMS has been used to induce changes in cortical oscillations.
source: Non-invasive stimulation via transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) and repeated transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been used to induce changes in cortical oscillations (Fröhlich, 2014), but the frequency of the induced oscillations was not solely dependent on the stimulation frequency (Marshall et al., 2006; Wach et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claim: The frequency of oscillations induced by tACS and rTMS was not solely dependent on the stimulation frequency.
source: Non-invasive stimulation via transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) and repeated transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been used to induce changes in cortical oscillations (Fröhlich, 2014), but the frequency of the induced oscillations was not solely dependent on the stimulation frequency (Marshall et al., 2006; Wach et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Reported changes in motor behavior from stimulation at beta frequencies are inconsistent.
source: Furthermore, the reported changes in motor behavior from stimulation at beta frequencies are inconsistent (Davis et al., 2012; Feurra et al., 2011; Pogosyan et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Three macaque monkeys with chronic microwire electrode arrays implanted in their motor cortices were trained in a sequential neurofeedback and arm-reaching task.
source: In this study, three macaque monkeys with chronic microwire electrode arrays implanted in their motor cortices were trained in a sequential neurofeedback and arm-reaching task.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the experimental setup.

claim: Sequential neurofeedback-behavior task designs have been used previously with a variety of neural recording modalities, neural signal features, and behaviors.
source: Sequential neurofeedback-behavior task designs have been used previously with a variety of neural recording modalities, neural signal features, and behaviors (Gevensleben et al., 2009; McFarland et al., 2015; Schafer and Moore, 2011; Subramanian et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Slowly oscillating ephaptic fields have been shown to entrain spiking behavior in vitro.
source: It has been suggested that the presence of beta oscillations either locally or distally could influence neuronal computation (Fries, 2015; Reimer and Hatsopoulos, 2010), as slowly oscillating ephaptic fields have been shown to entrain spiking behavior in vitro (Fröhlich and McCormick, 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to Fröhlich and McCormick, 2010.

claim: Little evidence exists showing that beta oscillations in the local field potential influence spiking activity through ephaptic mechanisms.
source: However, little evidence exists showing that beta oscillations in the local field potential influence spiking activity through ephaptic mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an assessment of the literature.

claim: Single cells are synchronized to ongoing beta oscillations but the strength of this synchronization is unrelated to the involvement of the neuron during the motor task.
source: Prior studies investigating neural activity changes during beta oscillations used acute, single-electrode recording preparations and showed that single cells are synchronized to ongoing oscillations but that the strength of this synchronization is unrelated to the involvement of the neuron during the motor task (Murthy and Fetz, 1996a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to Murthy and Fetz, 1996a.

claim: Individual cells do not change their mean spike firing rate but do exhibit a reduction in spiking variability during oscillations compared to before the oscillation.
source: These studies also show individual cells do not change their mean spike firing rate but do exhibit a reduction in spiking variability during oscillations compared to the variability exhibited before the oscillation (Murthy and Fetz, 1996b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to Murthy and Fetz, 1996b.

claim: There is substantial work linking spiking patterns to movement onset.
source: In contrast, if one were to omit the role that beta oscillations may play in motor behavior, there is substantial work linking spiking patterns to specific aspects of motor behavior such as movement onset (Kaufman et al., 2014), reaction time (Afshar et al., 2011; Churchland and Shenoy, 2007), movement angle (Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Lillicrap and Scott, 2013), and movement speed (Churchland et al., 2006; Moran and Schwartz, 1999), to list just a few.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to Kaufman et al., 2014.

claim: There is substantial work linking spiking patterns to reaction time.
source: In contrast, if one were to omit the role that beta oscillations may play in motor behavior, there is substantial work linking spiking patterns to specific aspects of motor behavior such as movement onset (Kaufman et al., 2014), reaction time (Afshar et al., 2011; Churchland and Shenoy, 2007), movement angle (Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Lillicrap and Scott, 2013), and movement speed (Churchland et al., 2006; Moran and Schwartz, 1999), to list just a few.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Afshar et al., 2011; Churchland and Shenoy, 2007.

claim: There is substantial work linking spiking patterns to movement angle.
source: In contrast, if one were to omit the role that beta oscillations may play in motor behavior, there is substantial work linking spiking patterns to specific aspects of motor behavior such as movement onset (Kaufman et al., 2014), reaction time (Afshar et al., 2011; Churchland and Shenoy, 2007), movement angle (Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Lillicrap and Scott, 2013), and movement speed (Churchland et al., 2006; Moran and Schwartz, 1999), to list just a few.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Lillicrap and Scott, 2013.

claim: There is substantial work linking spiking patterns to movement speed.
source: In contrast, if one were to omit the role that beta oscillations may play in motor behavior, there is substantial work linking spiking patterns to specific aspects of motor behavior such as movement onset (Kaufman et al., 2014), reaction time (Afshar et al., 2011; Churchland and Shenoy, 2007), movement angle (Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Lillicrap and Scott, 2013), and movement speed (Churchland et al., 2006; Moran and Schwartz, 1999), to list just a few.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Churchland et al., 2006; Moran and Schwartz, 1999.

claim: The clearest movement-related desynchronization was in the 25–40 Hz band for all monkeys.
source: A movement onset-aligned trial-averaged spectrogram from the intracortical recordings in contralateral motor and premotor cortex (e.g. Monkey C in Figure 1d) showed that the clearest movement-related desynchronization was in the 25–40 Hz band for all monkeys, consistent with early reports of beta oscillations in the macaque motor cortex (Baker et al., 1997; Murthy and Fetz, 1992).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1d and citations.

claim: The beta band limits for the neurofeedback epoch of the NR task were set at 25–40 Hz.
source: Thus, the beta band limits for the neurofeedback epoch of the NR task were set at 25–40 Hz.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a methodological decision.

claim: All three subjects perform the neurofeedback epoch part of the task above chance.
source: During NR task performance from these days, subjects exhibited above chance performance (Figure 1e, see Materials and methods - Chance level performance of beta neurofeedback epoch).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Monkeys achieved average success rates of 60% in the NR task.
source: Monkeys achieved average success rates of 60% and performed on average ~4 successful trials per minute.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a summary of performance data.

claim: Monkeys performed on average ~4 successful trials per minute in the NR task.
source: Monkeys achieved average success rates of 60% and performed on average ~4 successful trials per minute.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a summary of performance data.

claim: Errors almost entirely came from accidentally moving the right hand outside the center target during the neurofeedback epoch.
source: Errors almost entirely came from accidentally moving the right hand outside the center target during the neurofeedback epoch.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an observation of error types.

claim: At the time of the go cue there is a significant group difference in normalized beta power for the four different neurofeedback target conditions in Monkey S.
source: At the time of the go cue there is a significant group difference in normalized beta power for the four different neurofeedback target conditions (two-tailed Kruskal-Wallis test, Monkey S: n = 1184, H = 47.44, p=2.803e-10, Monkey C: n = 2328, H = 250.1, p<5e-20, Monkey G: n = 1042, H = 48.11, p=2.023e-10).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results.

claim: At the time of the go cue there is a significant group difference in normalized beta power for the four different neurofeedback target conditions in Monkey C.
source: At the time of the go cue there is a significant group difference in normalized beta power for the four different neurofeedback target conditions (two-tailed Kruskal-Wallis test, Monkey S: n = 1184, H = 47.44, p=2.803e-10, Monkey C: n = 2328, H = 250.1, p<5e-20, Monkey G: n = 1042, H = 48.11, p=2.023e-10).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results.

claim: At the time of the go cue there is a significant group difference in normalized beta power for the four different neurofeedback target conditions in Monkey G.
source: At the time of the go cue there is a significant group difference in normalized beta power for the four different neurofeedback target conditions (two-tailed Kruskal-Wallis test, Monkey S: n = 1184, H = 47.44, p=2.803e-10, Monkey C: n = 2328, H = 250.1, p<5e-20, Monkey G: n = 1042, H = 48.11, p=2.023e-10).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results.

claim: High and low beta targets were achieved by increasing and decreasing beta power, respectively.
source: Mean traces show that high and low beta targets were achieved by increasing and decreasing beta power, respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: In some subjects (Monkeys C, G), increases and decreases in beta power were accompanied by reliable decreases and increases in low frequencies (1–10 Hz).
source: In some subjects (Monkeys C, G), increases and decreases in beta power were accompanied by reliable decreases and increases in low frequencies (1–10 Hz).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: All subjects exhibit increasing percentages of on-beta time points for the low to high beta targets.
source: All subjects exhibit increasing percentages of on-beta time points for the low to high beta targets.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: In all three animals, trials with high beta power targets had subsequent reaches with slower movement onset times.
source: In all three animals, trials with high beta power targets had subsequent reaches with slower movement onset times (Figure 3a–c, two-tailed Cuzick's test, Monkey S: z = 5.763, p=8.267e-09, n = 1183, Monkey C: z = 11.987, p<5e-20, n = 2168, Monkey G: z = 5.856, p=4.729e-09, n = 1028).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results and Figure 3.

claim: Other groups have found increased beta power correlated with reduced movement onset speed, peak speed, and movement onset acceleration.
source: Other groups have found increased beta power correlated with reduced movement onset speed, peak speed, and movement onset acceleration (see Joundi et al., 2012; Pogosyan et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claim: The study did not find consistent correlations between beta power and movement onset speed, peak speed, and movement onset acceleration across subjects.
source: We did not find this consistently across subjects when comparing metrics grouped based on our proxy for beta power, the preceding beta target (see Table 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: For Monkeys S and G the time to acquire beta target did not significantly predict MOT in a linear regression.
source: For Monkeys S and G the time to acquire beta target did not significantly predict MOT in a linear regression, but it did for Monkey C and when data were combined across monkeys (Figure 4a–c two-sided Student's t-test for non-zero slope in linear regression, Monkey S: t = 0.7119, p=0.476, n = 1183, Monkey C: t = 2.352, p=0.0188, n = 2168, Monkey G: t = 1.651, p=0.0991, n = 1028, Combined across monkeys: t = 2.0832, p=0.0373, n = 4379).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results and Figure 4.

claim: Time to beta target significantly predicted MOT for Monkey C.
source: For Monkeys S and G the time to acquire beta target did not significantly predict MOT in a linear regression, but it did for Monkey C and when data were combined across monkeys (Figure 4a–c two-sided Student's t-test for non-zero slope in linear regression, Monkey S: t = 0.7119, p=0.476, n = 1183, Monkey C: t = 2.352, p=0.0188, n = 2168, Monkey G: t = 1.651, p=0.0991, n = 1028, Combined across monkeys: t = 2.0832, p=0.0373, n = 4379).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results and Figure 4.

claim: The slight predictive power of time to beta target on MOT does not account for increasing MOT with increasing beta target.
source: Thus, the slight predictive power of time to beta target on MOT does not account for increasing MOT with increasing beta target, as seen in Figure 3.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Changing the arm-reaching target location produces the same effect of increased MOT with increased beta target.
source: To test whether the beta target versus movement onset time relationship generalizes to more than a single arm-reaching target, Monkey S performed the original NR task, but with a different arm-reaching target location. Changing the arm-reaching target location produces the same effect (Figure 4d, Monkey S: z = 3.972, p=7.117e-05, n = 735).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results and Figure 4d.

claim: Reversing the relationship between beta target and screen location reverses the relationship between target number and MOT.
source: For these trials, the high beta power target became the green Target 1 instead of the red Target 4. Figure 4e shows that this manipulation reverses the relationship between target number and MOT (z = −5.971, p=2.354e-09, n = 2113) demonstrating that increasing beta power, not the target position on the screen, consistently correlates with the observed increasing movement onset time.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results and Figure 4e.

claim: All three monkeys exhibit significantly increasing movement onset times with increasing non-normalized beta power.
source: All three monkeys exhibit significantly increasing movement onset times with increasing non-normalized beta power (two-tailed Cuzick's test, Monkey S, z = 7.162, p=7.945e-13, n = 1183, Monkey C, z = 7.767, p=7.994e-15, n = 2168, Monkey G, z = 7.709 p=1.266e-14, n = 1028, Combined across monkeys: z = 6.168, p=6.924e-10, n = 4379).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results.

claim: Trials with a larger percentage of on-beta time points exhibit slower movement onset times.
source: Indeed, the same increase in movement onset time follows where trials with a larger percentage of on-beta time points exhibit slower movement onset times (two-tailed Cuzick's test, Monkey S, z = 7.575, p=3.597e-14, n = 1183, Monkey C, z = 5.488, p=4.068e-08, n = 2168, Monkey G, z = 7.890, p=3.108e-15, n = 1028, Combined across monkeys z = 5.1301, p=2.895e-07, n = 4379).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results.

claim: Increasing 10-25 Hz power correlates with increasing MOT.
source: Increasing 10-25 Hz power correlates with increasing MOT (two-tailed Cuzick's test, Monkey S 10–25 Hz: z = −0.6660, p=0.5054, n = 1183, Monkey C 10–25 Hz: z = 5.717, p=1.082e-08, n = 2168, Monkey G 10–25 Hz: z = 5.477, p=4.33e-08, n = 1028, Combined across monkeys 10–25 Hz: z = 2.9728, p=2.951e-03, n = 4379).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results.

claim: The 65–100 Hz (gamma) band exhibits consistently decreasing power for higher beta targets across monkeys.
source: The 65–100 Hz (gamma) band does exhibit consistently decreasing power for higher beta targets across monkeys (two-tailed Cuzick's test, Monkey S: z = −5.0279, p=4.96e-07, n = 1183, Monkey C: z = −4.227, p=2.368e-05, n = 2168, Monkey G: z = −1.775, p=0.0759, n = 1028, Combined across monkeys z = −3.1079, p=1.884e-03, n = 4379).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results.

claim: Beta power and gamma power have been shown to be anti-correlated in motor-related regions during tasks involving movement.
source: Indeed, beta power and gamma power have been shown to be anti-correlated in motor-related regions during tasks involving movement (Courtemanche et al., 2003; Schoffelen et al., 2005), in prefrontal cortex during working memory tasks (Lundqvist et al., 2016), and in parkinsonian subjects at rest (Fogelson et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Gamma power constitutes less than 3% of the total broadband estimate.
source: It is unlikely that subjects are relying on changes in gamma power, which would change the denominator term in the beta cursor computation, to drive their neurofeedback strategy as gamma power constitutes less than 3% of the total broadband estimate (Table 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data in Table 4.

claim: Beta power explains more MOT variance than gamma power.
source: Thus, while gamma power is negatively correlated with MOT, beta power explains more MOT variance than gamma power, and addition of beta power to a model predicting MOT with gamma power significantly improves prediction.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a conclusion from model comparison analysis.

claim: Addition of beta power to a model predicting MOT with gamma power significantly improves prediction.
source: Thus, while gamma power is negatively correlated with MOT, beta power explains more MOT variance than gamma power, and addition of beta power to a model predicting MOT with gamma power significantly improves prediction.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a conclusion from model comparison analysis.

claim: The 1–10 Hz band shows a consistent across-monkey decrease in movement onset time with increased power.
source: The 1–10 Hz band also shows a consistent across-monkey decrease in movement onset time with increased power, discussed further below (two-tailed Cuzick's test, Monkey S z = −4.290, p=1.785e-05, n = 1183, Monkey C: z = −6.8774, p=6.097 e-12, n = 2168, Monkey G: z = −8.4548, p=2.795e-17, n = 1028, Combined across monkeys z = −5.3049, p=1.127e-07, n = 4379).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results.

claim: In the beta task variant, Monkey G adopted a new strategy for getting to the lowest target.
source: In the beta task variant, Monkey G adopted a new strategy for getting to the lowest target.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: For the lowest (green) target in the beta task variant, Monkey G managed to increase the power of his beta frequencies to similar levels as the highest beta target (red).
source: For the lowest (green) target in the beta task variant, Monkey G managed to increase the power of his beta frequencies to similar levels as the highest beta target (red) but as he concomitantly increased the power of other frequencies, the denominator term in the normalized beta metric increased more, making the cursor move downwards (Figure 5i).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data in Figure 5i.

claim: The movement onset times followed beta power ordering, not 1–10 Hz power ordering in the task variant.
source: The movement onset times (Figure 5g, right) for the green target rose to match the movement onset times of the red target, indicating that the movement onset times followed beta power ordering, not 1–10 Hz power ordering (one-tailed Cuzick's test for significant ordering of beta targets in Figure 5g, right assesses increasing movement onset times per the group order 2, 3, 4, 1 instead of group order of 1, 2, 3, 4 used in all other Cuzick's tests. Monkey G: z = 7.1359, p=4.807e-13, n = 1164).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results and Figure 5g.

claim: Beta power explains more MOT variance than 1–10 Hz power.
source: Thus, while 1–10 Hz power is negatively correlated with MOT, beta power explains more MOT variance than 1–10 Hz power, and addition of beta power to a model predicting MOT with 1–10 Hz power significantly improves prediction.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a conclusion from model comparison analysis.

claim: Addition of beta power to a model predicting MOT with 1–10 Hz power significantly improves prediction.
source: Thus, while 1–10 Hz power is negatively correlated with MOT, beta power explains more MOT variance than 1–10 Hz power, and addition of beta power to a model predicting MOT with 1–10 Hz power significantly improves prediction.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a conclusion from model comparison analysis.

claim: Delta and theta bands, but not the alpha band, strongly correlate with MOT in all three animals.
source: By performing the same analysis as in Figure 5d–f with the narrower bands, we found that delta and theta bands, but not the alpha band, strongly correlate with MOT in all three animals (Monkey S: 1–3 Hz: z = −3.276, p=1.052e-03, n = 1183, 4–7 Hz: z = −3.245, p=1.174e-03, n = 1183, 8–12 Hz: z = −1.309, p=0.1907, n = 1183, Monkey C: 1–3 Hz: z = −6.986, p=2.821e-12, n = 2168, 4–7 Hz: z = −6.133, p=8.602e-10, n = 2168, 8–12 Hz: z = −1.779, p=0.0753, n = 2168, Monkey G, 1–3 Hz: z = −8.201, p=2.379e-16, n = 1028, 4–7 Hz: z = −6.166, p=7.024e-10, n = 1028, 8–12 Hz: z = 0.0669, p=0.9467, n = 1028, Combined over monkeys: 1–3 Hz: −5.006, p=5.55e-07, n = 4379, 4–7 Hz: z = −4.355, p=1.33e-05, n = 4379, 8–12 Hz: z = −0.9782, p=0.328, n = 4379).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results.

claim: Each day, 40–60% of units from Monkey G exhibited significantly different firing rates for NR versus CO slow, on-beta bins.
source: Each day, 40–60% of units from Monkey G (15–20% of units from Monkey C, inset) exhibited significantly different firing rates for NR versus CO slow, on-beta bins.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data analysis.

claim: 15–20% of units from Monkey C exhibited significantly different firing rates for NR versus CO slow, on-beta bins.
source: Each day, 40–60% of units from Monkey G (15–20% of units from Monkey C, inset) exhibited significantly different firing rates for NR versus CO slow, on-beta bins.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data analysis.

claim: For both CO and NR tasks, correlation coefficients for within-task beta-to-rate slope estimates exceed 0.8.
source: For both tasks, correlation coefficients exceed 0.8.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a summary of correlation analysis.

claim: High correlation coefficients suggest a stable within-task beta-to-rate mapping.
source: These high correlation coefficients suggest a stable within-task beta-to-rate mapping.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an interpretation of the correlation results.

claim: Across task slope estimates are less correlated across units than within-task slope estimates.
source: In contrast to the stable within-task slope estimates, across task slope estimates are less correlated across units.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: The mean firing rates of units during slow, on-beta timepoints are different for many units across CO and NR tasks.
source: Thus, the mean firing rates of units during slow, on-beta timepoints and the continuous beta amplitude-to-spike rate mappings across tasks are different for many units.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a summary of the analysis.

claim: The continuous beta amplitude-to-spike rate mappings across tasks are different for many units.
source: Thus, the mean firing rates of units during slow, on-beta timepoints and the continuous beta amplitude-to-spike rate mappings across tasks are different for many units.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a summary of the analysis.

claim: The same CO-trained classifier yields significantly different distances to MO threshold for PreMO and PostMO chunks in the NR task.
source: Instead, we confirm that the same CO-trained classifier does yield significantly different distances to MO threshold for PreMO and PostMO chunks in the NR task (Figure 7a, Red: NR task, paired two-tailed Student's t-test on mean within-day probabilities for CO PreMO and PostMO chunks, Monkey G: n = 6, T = −7.459, p=6.83e-04, Monkey C (inset): n = 4,T = −13.591, p=8.62e-04, Combined across monkeys: T = −3.6193, p=5.578e-03, n = 10).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results and Figure 7a.

claim: The population reliably encodes gross kinematics similarly across tasks despite individual unit activity changes.
source: This finding validates that the population reliably encodes gross kinematics similarly across tasks despite the individual unit activity changes observed across tasks in the previous analysis.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an interpretation of the classifier results.

claim: Off-beta slow chunks exhibit significantly closer distances to MO threshold than on-beta slow chunks in all cases but one.
source: In all cases but one, off-beta slow chunks exhibit significantly closer distances to MO threshold than on-beta slow chunks (paired Students' t-test of within-day means Figure 7d: Monkey G: CO off-beta vs. on-beta, n = 6, T = 6.742, p=1.089e-03, NR off-beta vs. on-beta, n = 6, T = 2.607, p=0.0478, Figure 7e: Monkey C: CO off-beta vs. on-beta, n = 4, T = 1.325, p=0.277 NR off-beta vs. on-beta n = 4, T = 4.763, p=0.0176, Combined across monkeys: CO off-beta vs. on-beta, n = 10, T = 4.246, p=2.160e-03, NF off-beta vs. on-beta, n = 10, T = 3.185, p=0.0111).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical test results and Figures 7d-e.

claim: The CO and NR tasks exhibit common population-level activity changes reflected by the onset of beta oscillations.
source: The CO and NR tasks exhibit common population-level activity changes reflected by the onset of beta oscillations, and specifically, these population changes encode a shift further away from the MO threshold.
